Level: B1+/B2
Time: 60 minutes
Dialect: British English
Goal: to develop students' ability to identify textual evidence, recognise paraphrasing and eliminate distractors in EGE Reading Tasks 12–18, and discuss trust, friendship and social media
Reading: EGE Tasks 12–18
Vocabulary: expressions related to unexpected experiences, relationships and public attention
Speaking: evaluating decisions, expressing and justifying opinions, responding to opposing arguments

• get on with your life — to continue living normally after something difficult or unusual has happened
  • take a chance on someone — to trust someone or give them an opportunity, even though you are not sure what will happen
  • lose interest in something — to stop being interested in something that previously attracted your attention
  • keep something to yourself — to avoid telling other people about something, especially personal information
  • reach a wider audience — to make information, a story or an idea available to more people
  • offer practical support — to help someone by doing useful things rather than just giving advice or encouragement

Show the photograph without revealing how the two people met. Ask: "What do you notice about these people? What kind of relationship might they have?" Show the photograph and ask students to vote individually. Invite two students with different choices to explain their predictions. Keep this brief; do not confirm the correct option yet.

The Thanksgiving Invitation That Changed Two Lives

Most wrong-number messages are quickly forgotten. The recipient explains the mistake, the sender apologises, and both get on with their lives. But when Arizona grandmother Wanda Dench accidentally invited a teenager called Jamal Hinton to Thanksgiving dinner, neither could have imagined how much that brief exchange would change their lives. What began as an unlikely invitation has developed into a friendship that has lasted for a decade — and attracted an audience of millions.

Dench had intended to contact her grandson, but the message reached Hinton instead. Rather than ignore it, the teenager tried to work out who was texting him. Once the confusion had been cleared up, he jokingly asked whether the invitation was still open. To his surprise, Dench welcomed him anyway. Hinton accepted, and a simple family dinner became the beginning of an annual tradition. The encounter challenged the sort of assumptions that might normally prevent two strangers, separated by generations, from meeting at all. Their initial willingness to take a chance on each other would prove far more significant than either realised.

As photographs of their Thanksgiving gatherings spread online, the pair gradually became familiar faces to people who had never met them. For Hinton, the attention was an unexpected pleasure. He had imagined becoming famous when he was younger, although he could hardly have predicted that an accidental text would make it happen. Dench was less comfortable with the publicity at first. She worried that the public might eventually lose interest or become irritated by their continued appearances in the news. Over time, however, the encouraging messages they received persuaded her that their story still had something worthwhile to offer. She began to regard the attention less as an intrusion and more as an opportunity to make others happy.

Yet the most important developments in the friendship happened away from the cameras. The two began spending time together on birthdays and other occasions, not just Thanksgiving. Their relationship was also tested by loss. When Dench's husband, Lonnie, died in 2020, Hinton and his partner visited her home and left a basket outside, observing the social-distancing restrictions in place at the time. The gesture could not take away her grief, but it showed that their friendship was no longer dependent on an annual celebration. Hinton has continued to remember Lonnie publicly each November, recognising the part he played in the tradition from its earliest years.

Another difficult period followed when Dench was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2023. She had initially considered keeping the diagnosis to herself. However, she realised that sharing her experience might encourage other women to attend medical screenings. Hinton supported her decision by helping the message reach a wider audience after she had lost access to her original social-media account. Dench has since reported that she is cancer-free. What had started as an online curiosity had become a relationship in which both people were prepared to offer practical support when it mattered.

Their lives continue to move in different directions. Dench has retired and is considering how she would like to spend her time, while Hinton is involved in several professional and community projects. They do not share the same background or generation, and they have never pretended otherwise. Nevertheless, the friendship has given them something neither was searching for when the first message arrived. To the millions following their story, their annual Thanksgiving photograph may be a cheerful holiday tradition. For the two people in it, however, the dinner is only one small part of a much deeper connection.
12. What point does the writer make in the opening paragraph?
Messages sent to the wrong person often lead to misunderstandings between relatives.
An apparently insignificant accident can have unexpectedly lasting consequences.
People are more likely to form friendships online than at family gatherings.

12. What point does the writer make in the opening paragraph?
  • Messages sent to the wrong person often lead to misunderstandings between relatives.
  • An apparently insignificant accident can have unexpectedly lasting consequences. ✓
  • People are more likely to form friendships online than at family gatherings.
  • Public attention is usually necessary for an unusual friendship to survive.
13. What was unusual about Jamal's response to the invitation?
  • He accepted it before realising that the message had been sent by mistake.
  • He immediately invited Wanda to meet his own family instead.
  • He assumed that Wanda was deliberately trying to contact him.
  • The mistake did not discourage him from asking whether he could attend. ✓
14. What prompted Wanda to reconsider her attitude towards publicity?
  • Positive reactions convinced her that their story brought happiness to others. ✓
  • Jamal's enthusiasm for becoming famous encouraged her to enjoy the attention.
  • The media began to show less interest in their annual celebrations.
  • She realised the publicity could create new professional opportunities.
15. Why does the writer mention the basket left outside Wanda's home?
  • To explain why the two friends stopped visiting each other regularly.
  • To suggest that social-distancing rules made personal support impossible.
  • To demonstrate that their friendship involved support beyond Thanksgiving dinners. ✓
  • To show that the loss of Wanda's husband brought their tradition to an end.
16. Why did Wanda eventually decide to speak publicly about her illness?
  • Her followers had repeatedly asked her to explain her absence from social media.
  • She hoped her experience would encourage other women to have medical screenings. ✓
  • Jamal had persuaded her that sharing personal information was necessary.
  • She wanted to reassure people that future Thanksgiving gatherings would continue.
17. What does the writer suggest by contrasting Wanda's and Jamal's current lives?
  • Their professional commitments are gradually making the friendship less important.
  • They have begun planning similar careers because of their shared experiences.
  • Their online popularity has forced them both to reconsider their future plans.
  • Their different circumstances have not prevented them from remaining close. ✓
18. What idea does the writer emphasise at the end of the article?
  • The public sees a holiday tradition, but the relationship means much more to the people involved. ✓
  • The friendship has lasted mainly because the two continue to attract online attention.
  • Their different backgrounds have become less important because of their shared interests.
  • The annual dinner has remained the most meaningful part of their relationship.

The Thanksgiving Invitation That Changed Two Lives

Most wrong-number messages are quickly forgotten. The recipient explains the mistake, the sender apologises, and both get on with their lives. But when Arizona grandmother Wanda Dench accidentally invited a teenager called Jamal Hinton to Thanksgiving dinner, neither could have imagined how much that brief exchange would change their lives. What began as an unlikely invitation has developed into a friendship that has lasted for a decade — and attracted an audience of millions.

Dench had intended to contact her grandson, but the message reached Hinton instead. Rather than ignore it, the teenager tried to work out who was texting him. Once the confusion had been cleared up, he jokingly asked whether the invitation was still open. To his surprise, Dench welcomed him anyway. Hinton accepted, and a simple family dinner became the beginning of an annual tradition. The encounter challenged the sort of assumptions that might normally prevent two strangers, separated by generations, from meeting at all. Their initial willingness to take a chance on each other would prove far more significant than either realised.

As photographs of their Thanksgiving gatherings spread online, the pair gradually became familiar faces to people who had never met them. For Hinton, the attention was an unexpected pleasure. He had imagined becoming famous when he was younger, although he could hardly have predicted that an accidental text would make it happen. Dench was less comfortable with the publicity at first. She worried that the public might eventually lose interest or become irritated by their continued appearances in the news. Over time, however, the encouraging messages they received persuaded her that their story still had something worthwhile to offer. She began to regard the attention less as an intrusion and more as an opportunity to make others happy.

Yet the most important developments in the friendship happened away from the cameras. The two began spending time together on birthdays and other occasions, not just Thanksgiving. Their relationship was also tested by loss. When Dench's husband, Lonnie, died in 2020, Hinton and his partner visited her home and left a basket outside, observing the social-distancing restrictions in place at the time. The gesture could not take away her grief, but it showed that their friendship was no longer dependent on an annual celebration. Hinton has continued to remember Lonnie publicly each November, recognising the part he played in the tradition from its earliest years.

Another difficult period followed when Dench was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2023. She had initially considered keeping the diagnosis to herself. However, she realised that sharing her experience might encourage other women to attend medical screenings. Hinton supported her decision by helping the message reach a wider audience after she had lost access to her original social-media account. Dench has since reported that she is cancer-free. What had started as an online curiosity had become a relationship in which both people were prepared to offer practical support when it mattered.

Their lives continue to move in different directions. Dench has retired and is considering how she would like to spend her time, while Hinton is involved in several professional and community projects. They do not share the same background or generation, and they have never pretended otherwise. Nevertheless, the friendship has given them something neither was searching for when the first message arrived. To the millions following their story, their annual Thanksgiving photograph may be a cheerful holiday tradition. For the two people in it, however, the dinner is only one small part of a much deeper connection.
12. What point does the writer make in the opening paragraph?
Messages sent to the wrong person often lead to misunderstandings between relatives.
An apparently insignificant accident can have unexpectedly lasting consequences.
People are more likely to form friendships online than at family gatherings.

parts.title: Read the text and complete Tasks 12–18.
parts.html:
More Than a Thanksgiving Dinner

For many Americans, Thanksgiving means travelling to see relatives, preparing a familiar meal and spending the afternoon around a table. In Watertown, New York, however, a different kind of gathering takes place every year. At the local Salvation Army centre, volunteers give up part of their holiday to make sure people they may never have met can enjoy a Thanksgiving dinner. In 2025, the event brought together people with very different circumstances, but a shared willingness to help.

Preparations began well before Thursday's meal. The organisers were expecting to provide nearly 2,000 dinners, around 800 more than the previous year. The increase was not an attempt to break a record. With more local residents struggling financially, the organisers believed the demand for free meals would be higher. Some people could come to the centre and eat there; others would receive food delivered to them. Getting hundreds of additional meals ready required more than a few enthusiastic cooks.

Among approximately 100 volunteers was 15-year-old Nadji Booker, who had been involved since he was four. His role that morning was serving guests who arrived at the centre. Over the years, he had come to recognise fellow volunteers and some of the people who returned for dinner each Thanksgiving. What might look to an outsider like work among strangers felt to him more like spending time with an extended family. He particularly valued the knowledge that he was doing something useful for someone else. Unlike many teenagers who might be trying volunteering for the first time, Nadji had grown up with it as part of his holiday routine.

Katherine Bull was a newcomer to the event, and her circumstances were quite different. While Nadji welcomed guests, she packed meals to be delivered elsewhere. Katherine was experiencing homelessness herself, yet she chose to spend the holiday helping people she considered less fortunate. She did not suggest that volunteering had solved her own problems. Instead, helping others gave her a chance to appreciate what she still had. Her story challenges the assumption that the people offering help and those who need it always belong to separate groups.

Money was another concern. Shortly before Thanksgiving, a local community foundation provided $19,000 to the Salvation Army: $4,000 for the holiday meal and $15,000 towards replacing a delivery van. Captain Joshua Morales explained that paying for a vehicle without outside support could have meant taking money away from other services, such as the food pantry or soup kitchen. In other words, something would have had to give. Food donations from residents also helped keep costs down, making the operation a community effort rather than the work of one organisation alone.

Morales was particularly grateful to the volunteers. Some had brought food, others had prepared it, and still others served meals or delivered them. He emphasised that the dinner depended on all these contributions, not just on those seen speaking to guests. The work did not necessarily end when the tables were cleared, either: leftover food was to be distributed to people in need over the following days.

It would be easy to judge an event like this simply by counting the meals served. Those numbers matter, especially when more people need assistance. But the experiences of Nadji and Katherine suggest that Thanksgiving volunteering can mean something different to each person. One volunteer finds a familiar community; another finds a way to give despite facing difficulties herself. The meal is the reason everyone comes together, but it is not the only thing they take away from the day.

12. What is the purpose of the first paragraph?
  • To criticise the way American families usually celebrate Thanksgiving.
  • To introduce an alternative way of celebrating a traditional holiday. ✓
  • To explain why many Americans prefer to travel during Thanksgiving.
  • To suggest that volunteering is replacing family celebrations in the USA.
13. Why were the organisers planning to prepare more meals than the previous year?
  • They wanted to offer a greater variety of traditional dishes.
  • More volunteers had offered to help than they had expected.
  • The organisation hoped to attract public attention by breaking a record.
  • They anticipated greater demand because more people were experiencing financial difficulties. ✓
14. What does Nadji's experience of volunteering suggest?
  • Regular participation has helped him develop a sense of belonging. ✓
  • He returns mainly because he enjoys meeting new people every year.
  • He regards volunteering primarily as preparation for his future career.
  • He considers serving meals more important than making guests feel welcome.
15. What makes Katherine's decision to volunteer particularly remarkable?
  • She had previously received help from the same organisation.
  • She believed that volunteering would solve her personal problems.
  • She wanted to help others despite facing serious difficulties herself. ✓
  • She had been volunteering for years but was trying a different role.
16. The phrase something would have had to give in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to...
  • more people would have needed to donate food to the organisation.
  • one of the organisation's existing services would have suffered. ✓
  • the community foundation would have withdrawn its financial support.
  • the Salvation Army would have stopped delivering meals permanently.
17. Which of the following statements is FALSE, according to the text?
  • People could either eat at the centre or receive meals by delivery.
  • The community foundation provided funding for both food and transport needs.
  • Different kinds of voluntary work contributed to the success of the event.
  • The organisers planned to store leftover food for the following year's dinner. ✓
18. What is the main idea the writer expresses in the final paragraph?
  • Community volunteering can provide both practical help and a sense of connection. ✓
  • The success of a charity event should be measured primarily by the number of meals served.
  • People who volunteer regularly benefit more than those who help only once.
  • Thanksgiving is more meaningful when people celebrate it outside their own families.
